entries.868cc101c6e49040e51cf855f4cbcb0712340a2e: <div sID="gen31884" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Eph.6" sID="Eph.6"/> <div eID="gen31884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31885" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31886" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The apostle proceeds in the exhortation to relative duties which he began in the former, particularly he insists on the duties of children and parents, and of servants and masters, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.1-Eph.6.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. He exhorts and directs Christians how to behave themselves in the spiritual warfare with the enemies of their souls; and to the exercise of several Christian graces, which he proposes to them as so many pieces of spiritual armour, to preserve and defend them in the conflict, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.10-Eph.6.18">ver. 10-18</reference>. III. We have here the conclusion of the epistle, in which he takes his leave of them, recommending himself to the prayers of the believing Ephesians, and praying for them, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19-Eph.6.24">ver. 19-24</reference>.
entries.f0cc9ddd498914c8709b4a4aa1916590016caee8: <div eID="gen31886" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31885" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Duties of Children to Parents; Duties of Servants to Masters. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31887" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right. <hi type="super">2</hi> Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;) <hi type="super">3</hi> That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth. <hi type="super">4</hi> And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. <hi type="super">5</hi> Servants, be obedient to them that are <hi type="italic">your</hi> masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ; <hi type="super">6</hi> Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart; 7 With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men: <hi type="super">8</hi> Knowing that whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord, whether <hi type="italic">he be</hi> bond or free. <hi type="super">9</hi> And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him. <div eID="gen31887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31888" type="x-p"/> Here we have further directions concerning relative duties, in which the apostle is very particular. <div eID="gen31888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31889" type="x-p"/> I. The duty of children to their parents. <hi type="italic">Come, you children, hearken to me, I will teach you the fear of the Lord.</hi> The great duty of children is to obey their parents (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.1">v. 1</reference>), parents being the instruments of their being, God and nature having given them an authority to command, in subserviency to God; and, if children will be obedient to their pious parents, they will be in a fair way to be pious as they are. That obedience which God demands from their children, in their behalf, includes an inward reverence, as well as the outward expressions and acts. Obey in the Lord. Some take this as a limitation, and understand it thus: "as far as is consistent with your duty to God." We must not disobey our heavenly Father in obedience to earthly parents; for our obligation to God is prior and superior to all others. I take it rather as a reason: "Children, obey your parents; for the Lord has commanded it: obey them therefore for the Lord's sake, and with an eye to him." Or it may be a particular specification of the general duty: "Obey your parents, especially in those things which relate to the Lord. Your parents teach you good manners, and therein you must obey them. They teach you what is for your health, and in this you must obey them: but the chief things in which you are to do it are the things pertaining to the Lord." Religious parents charge their children to keep the ways of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen. xviii. 19</reference>. They command them to be found in the way of their duty towards God, and to take heed of those sins most incident to their age; in these things especially they must see that they be obedient. There is a general reason given: <hi type="italic">For this is right,</hi> there is a natural equity in it, God has enjoined it, and it highly becomes Christians. It is the order of nature that parents command and children obey. Though this may seem a hard saying, yet it is duty, and it must be done by such as would please God and approve themselves to him. For the proof of this the apostle quotes the law of the fifth commandment, which Christ was so far from designing to abrogate and repeal that he came to confirm it, as appears by his vindicating it, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.4">Matt. xv. 4</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">Honour thy father and mother</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.2">v. 2</reference>), which honour implies reverence, obedience, and relief and maintenance, if these be needed. The apostle adds, <hi type="italic">which is the first commandment with promise.</hi> Some little difficulty arises from this, which we should not overlook, because some who plead for the lawfulness of images bring this as a proof that we are not bound by <hi type="italic">the second commandment.</hi> But there is no manner of force in the argument. The second commandment has not a particular promise; but only a general declaration or assertion, which relates to the whole law of God's keeping mercy for thousands. And then by this is not meant the first commandment of the decalogue that has a promise, for there is no other after it that has, and therefore it would be improper to say it is the first; but the meaning may be this: "This is a prime or chief commandment, and it has a promise; it is the first commandment in the second table, and it has a promise." The promise is, <hi type="italic">That it may be well with thee,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.6.3">v. 3</reference>. Observe, Whereas the promise in the commandment has reference to the land of Canaan, the apostle hereby shows that this and other promises which we have in the Old Testament relating to the land of Canaan are to be understood more generally. That you may not think that the Jews only, to whom God gave the land of Canaan, were bound by the fifth commandment, he here gives it a further sense, <hi type="italic">That it may be well with thee,</hi> &c. Outward prosperity and long life are blessings promised to those who keep this commandment. This is the way to have it well with us, and obedient children are often rewarded with outward prosperity. Not indeed that it is always so; there are instances of such children who meet with much affliction in this life: but <hi type="italic">ordinarily</hi> obedience is thus rewarded, and, where it is not, it is made up with something better. Observe, 1. The gospel has its temporal promises, as well as spiritual ones. 2. Although the authority of God be sufficient to engage us in our duty, yet we are allowed to have respect to the promised reward: and, 3. Though it contains some temporal advantage, even this may be considered as a motive and encouragement to our obedience. <div eID="gen31889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31890" type="x-p"/> II. The duty of parents: <hi type="italic">And you fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.4">v. 4</reference>. Or, you parents, 1. "<hi type="italic">Do not provoke your children to wrath.</hi> Though God has given you power, you must not abuse that power, remembering that your children are, in a particular manner, pieces of yourselves, and therefore ought to be governed with great tenderness and love. Be not impatient with them, use no unreasonable severities and lay no rigid injunctions upon them. When you caution them, when you counsel them, when you reprove them, do it in such a manner as not to <hi type="italic">provoke them to wrath.</hi> In all such cases deal prudently and wisely with them, endeavouring to convince their judgments and to work upon their reason." 2. "<hi type="italic">Bring them up</hi> well, <hi type="italic">in the nurture and admonition of the Lord,</hi> in the discipline of proper and of compassionate correction, and in the knowledge of that duty which God requires of them and by which they may become better acquainted with him. Give them a good education." It is the great duty of parents to be careful in the education of their children: "Not only bring them up, as the brutes do, taking care to provide for them; but bring them up in nurture and admonition, in such a manner as is suitable to their reasonable natures. Nay, not only bring them up as men, in nurture and admonition, but as Christians, in the admonition of the Lord. Let them have a religious education. Instruct them to fear sinning; and inform them of, and excite them to, the whole of their duty towards God." <div eID="gen31890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31891" type="x-p"/> III. The duty of servants. This also is summed up in one word, which is, <hi type="italic">obedience.</hi> He is largest on this article, as knowing there was the greatest need of it. These servants were generally slaves. Civil servitude is not inconsistent with Christian liberty. Those may be the Lord's freemen who are slaves to men. "<hi type="italic">Your masters according to the flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">v. 5</reference>), that is, who have the command of your bodies, but not of your souls and consciences: God alone has dominion over these." Now, with respect to servants, he exhorts, 1. That they obey <hi type="italic">with fear and trembling.</hi> They are to reverence those who are over them, fearing to displease them, and trembling lest they should justly incur their anger and indignation. 2. That they be sincere in their obedience: <hi type="italic">In singleness of heart;</hi> not pretending obedience when they design disobedience, but serving them with faithfulness. 3. They should have an eye to Jesus Christ in all the service that they perform to their masters (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5-Eph.6.7">v. 5-7</reference>), <hi type="italic">doing service as to the Lord, and not to men;</hi> that is, not to men only or principally. When servants, in the discharge of the duty of their places, have an eye to Christ, this puts an honour upon their obedience, and an acceptableness into it. Service done to their earthly masters, with an eye to him, becomes acceptable service to him also. To have an eye to Christ is to remember that he sees them and is ever present with them, and that his authority obliges them to a faithful and conscientious discharge of the duties of their station. 4. They must not serve their masters <hi type="italic">with eye-service</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.6">v. 6</reference>)—that is, only when their master's eye is upon them; but they must be as conscientious in the discharge of their duty, when they are absent and out of the way, because then their Master in heaven beholds them: and therefore they must not act as <hi type="italic">men-pleasers</hi>—as though they had no regard to the pleasing of God, and approving themselves to him, if they can impose upon their masters. Observe, A steady regard to the Lord Jesus Christ will make men faithful and sincere in every station of life. 5. What they do they must do cheerfully: <hi type="italic">Doing the will of God from the heart,</hi> serving their masters as God wills they should, not grudgingly, nor by constraint, but from a principle of love to them and their concerns. This is <hi type="italic">doing it with good-will</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.7">v. 7</reference>), which will make their service easy to themselves, pleasing to their masters, and acceptable to the Lord Christ. There should be <hi type="italic">good-will</hi> to their masters, good-will to the families they are in; and especially a readiness to do their duty to God. Observe, Service, performed with conscience, and from a regard to God, though it be to unrighteous masters, will be accounted by Christ as service done to himself. 6. Let faithful servants trust God for their wages, while they do their duty in his fear: <hi type="italic">Knowing that whatsoever good thing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.8">v. 8</reference>), how poor and mean soever it may be, considered in itself,—<hi type="italic">the same shall he receive of the Lord,</hi> that is, by a metonymy, the reward of the same. Though his master on earth should neglect or abuse him, instead of rewarding him, he shall certainly be rewarded by the Lord Christ, <hi type="italic">whether he be bond or free,</hi> whether he be a poor bond-servant or a freeman or master. Christ regards not these differences of men at present; nor will he in the great and final judgment. You think, "A prince, or a magistrate, or a minister, that does his duty here, will be sure to receive his reward in heaven: but what capacity am I, a poor servant, in, of recommending myself to the favour of God." Why, God will as certainly reward thee for the meanest drudgery that is done from a sense of duty and with an eye to himself. And what can be said more proper either to engage or to encourage servants to their duty? <div eID="gen31891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31892" type="x-p"/> IV. The duty of masters: "<hi type="italic">And you masters, do the same things unto them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">v. 9</reference>); that is, act after the same manner. Be just to them, as you expect they should be to you: show the like good-will and concern for them, and be careful herein to approve yourselves to God." Observe, Masters are under as strict obligations to discharge their duty to their servants as servants are to be obedient and dutiful to them. "<hi type="italic">Forbearing threatening;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anientes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">moderating</hi> threatening, and remitting the evils with which you threaten them. Remember that your servants are made of the same mould with yourselves, and therefore be not tyrannical and imperious over them, <hi type="italic">knowing that your Master also is in heaven:</hi>" some copies read, both <hi type="italic">your</hi> and <hi type="italic">their</hi> Master. "You have a Master to obey who makes this your duty; and you and they are but fellow-servants in respect of Christ. You will be as punishable by him, for the neglect of your duty, or for acting contrary to it, as any others of meaner condition in the world. You are therefore to show favour to others, as ever you expect to find favour with him; and you will never be a match for him, though you may be too hard for your servants." <hi type="italic">Neither is there respect of persons with him;</hi> a rich, a wealthy, and a dignified master, if he be unjust, imperious, and abusive, is not a jot the nearer being accepted of God for his riches, wealth, and honour. He will call masters and servants to an impartial account for their conduct one to another, and will neither spare the former because they are more advanced nor be severe towards the latter because they are inferior and mean in the world. If both masters and servants would consider their relation and obligation to God and the account they must shortly give to him, they would be more careful of their duty to each other. Thus the apostle concludes his exhortation to relative duties.
entries.1195ab203661507be8af720f6c34114b9338ea46: <div eID="gen31892" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Spiritual Warfare. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31893" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. <hi type="super">11</hi> Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. 12 For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high <hi type="italic">places.</hi> 13 Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. <hi type="super">14</hi> Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness; <hi type="super">15</hi> And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; 16 Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. <hi type="super">17</hi> And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God: <hi type="super">18</hi> Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints; <div eID="gen31893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31894" type="x-p"/> Here is a general exhortation to constancy in our Christian course, and to encourage in our Christian warfare. Is not our life a warfare? It is so; for we struggle with the common calamities of human life. Is not our religion much more a warfare? It is so; for we struggle with the opposition of the powers of darkness, and with many enemies who would keep us from God and heaven. We have enemies to fight against, a captain to fight for, a banner to fight under, and certain rules of war by which we are to govern ourselves. "<hi type="italic">Finally, my brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.10">v. 10</reference>), it yet remains that you apply yourselves to your work and duty as Christian soldiers." Now it is requisite that a soldier be both stout-hearted and well armed. If Christians be soldiers of Jesus Christ, <div eID="gen31894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31895" type="x-p"/> I. They must see that they be stout-hearted. This is prescribed here: <hi type="italic">Be strong in the Lord,</hi> &c. Those who have so many battles to fight, and who, in their way to heaven, must dispute every pass, with dint of sword, have need of a great deal of courage. <hi type="italic">Be strong therefore,</hi> strong for service, strong for suffering, strong for fighting. Let a soldier be ever so well armed without, if he have not within a good heart, his armour will stand him in little stead. Note, spiritual strength and courage are very necessary for our spiritual warfare. Be strong in the Lord, either in his cause and for his sake or rather in his strength. We have no sufficient strength of our own. Our natural courage is as perfect cowardice, and our natural strength as perfect weakness; but all our sufficiency is of God. In his strength we must go forth and go on. By the actings of faith, we must fetch in grace and help from heaven to enable us to do that which of ourselves we cannot do, in our Christian work and warfare. We should stir up ourselves to resist temptations in a reliance upon God's all-sufficiency and the omnipotence of his might. <div eID="gen31895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31896" type="x-p"/> II. They must be well armed: "<hi type="italic">Put on the whole armour of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">v. 11</reference>), make use of all the proper defensitives and weapons for repelling the temptations and stratagems of Satan—get and exercise all the Christian graces, the whole armour, that no part be naked and exposed to the enemy." Observe, Those who would approve themselves to have true grace must aim at all grace, the whole armour. It is called the armour of God, because he both prepares and bestows it. We have no armour of our own that will be armour of proof in a trying time. Nothing will stand us in stead but the armour of God. This armour is prepared for us, but we must put it on; that is, we must pray for grace, we must use the grace given us, and draw it out into act and exercise as there is occasion. The reason assigned why the Christian should be completely armed is <hi type="italic">that he may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil</hi>—that he may be able to hold out, and to overcome, notwithstanding all the devil's assaults, both of force and fraud, all the deceits he puts upon us, all the snares he lays for us, and all his machinations against us. This the apostle enlarges upon here, and shows, <div eID="gen31896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31897" type="x-p"/> 1. What our danger is, and what need we have to put on this whole armour, considering what sort of enemies we have to deal with—the devil and all the powers of darkness: <hi type="italic">For we wrestle not against flesh and blood,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">v. 12</reference>. The combat for which we are to be prepared is not against ordinary human enemies, not barely against men compounded of <hi type="italic">flesh and blood,</hi> nor against our own corrupt natures singly considered, but against the several ranks of devils, who have a government which they exercise in this world. (1.) We have to do with a subtle enemy, an enemy who uses wiles and stratagems, as <reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">v. 11</reference>. He has a thousand ways of beguiling unstable souls: hence he is called a serpent for subtlety, an old serpent, experienced in the art and trade of tempting. (2.) He is a powerful enemy: <hi type="italic">Principalities,</hi> and <hi type="italic">powers,</hi> and <hi type="italic">rulers.</hi> They are numerous, they are vigorous; and rule in those heathen nations which are yet in darkness. The dark parts of the world are the seat of Satan's empire. Yea, they are usurping princes over all men who are yet in a state of sin and ignorance. Satan's is a kingdom of darkness; whereas Christ's is a kingdom of light. (3.) They are spiritual enemies: <hi type="italic">Spiritual wickedness in high places,</hi> or wicked spirits, as some translate it. The devil is a spirit, a wicked spirit; and our danger is the greater from our enemies because they are unseen, and assault us ere we are aware of them. The devils are wicked spirits, and they chiefly annoy the saints with, and provoke them to, spiritual wickednesses, pride, envy, malice, &c. These enemies are said to be <hi type="italic">in high places,</hi> or in heavenly places, so the word is, taking heaven (as one says) for the whole <hi type="italic">expansum,</hi> or spreading out of the air between the earth and the stars, the air being the place from which the devils assault us. Or the meaning may be, "<hi type="italic">We wrestle</hi> about heavenly places or heavenly things;" so some of the ancients interpret it. Our enemies strive to prevent our ascent to heaven, to deprive us of heavenly blessings and to obstruct our communion with heaven. They assault us in the things that belong to our souls, and labour to deface the heavenly image in our hearts; and therefore we have need to be upon our guard against them. We have need of faith in our Christian warfare, because we have spiritual enemies to grapple with, as well as of faith in our Christian work, because we have spiritual strength to fetch in. Thus you see your danger. <div eID="gen31897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31898" type="x-p"/> 2. What our duty is: to take and put on the whole armour of God, and then to stand our ground, and withstand our enemies. <div eID="gen31898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31899" type="x-p"/> (1.) We must <hi type="italic">withstand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">v. 13</reference>. We must not yield to the devil's allurements and assaults, but oppose them. Satan is said <hi type="italic">to stand up against us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.1">1 Chron. xxi. 1</reference>. If he stand up against us, we must stand against him; set up, and keep up, an interest in opposition to the devil. Satan is the wicked one, and his kingdom is the kingdom of sin: to stand against Satan is to strive against sin. <hi type="italic">That you may be able to withstand in the evil day,</hi> in the day of temptation, or of any sore affliction. <div eID="gen31899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31900" type="x-p"/> (2.) We must stand our ground: <hi type="italic">And, having done all, to stand.</hi> We must resolve, by God's grace, not to yield to Satan. Resist him, and he will flee. If we distrust our cause, or our leader, or our armour, we give him advantage. Our present business is to withstand the assaults of the devil, and to stand it out; and then, having done all that is incumbent on the good soldiers of Jesus Christ, our warfare will be accomplished, and we shall be finally victorious. <div eID="gen31900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31901" type="x-p"/> (3.) We must stand armed; and this is here most enlarged upon. Here is a Christian in complete armour: and the armour is divine: <hi type="italic">Armour of God, armour of light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Rom. xiii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Armour of righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.7">2 Cor. vi. 7</reference>. The apostle specifies the particulars of this armour, both offensive and defensive. The military girdle or belt, the breast-plate, the greaves (or soldier's shoes), the shield, the helmet, and the sword. It is observable that, among them all, there is none for the back; if we turn our back upon the enemy, we lie exposed. [1.] Truth or sincerity is our girdle, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.14">v. 14</reference>. It was prophesied of Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.5">Isa. xi. 5</reference>) that <hi type="italic">righteousness should be the girdle of his loins and faithfulness the girdle of his reins.</hi> That which Christ was girded with all Christians must be girded with. God desires truth, that is, sincerity, in the inward parts. This is the strength of our loins; and it girds on all other pieces of our armour, and therefore is first mentioned. I know no religion without sincerity. Some understand it of the doctrine of the truths of the gospel: they should cleave to us as the girdle does to the loins, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>. This will restrain from libertinism and licentiousness, as a girdle restrains and keeps in the body. This is the Christian soldier's belt: ungirded with this, he is unblessed. [2.] Righteousness must be our breast-plate. The breast-plate secures the vitals, shelters the heart. The righteousness of Christ imputed to us is our breast-plate against the arrows of divine wrath. The righteousness of Christ implanted in us is our breast-plate to fortify the heart against the attacks which Satan makes against us. The apostle explains this in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1 Thess. v. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">Putting on the breast-plate of faith and love.</hi> Faith and love include all Christian graces; for by faith we are united to Christ and by love to our brethren. These will infer a diligent observance of our duty to God, and a righteous deportment towards men, in all the offices of justice, truth, and charity. [3.] Resolution must be as the greaves to our legs: <hi type="italic">And their feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.15">v. 15</reference>. Shoes, or greaves of brass, or the like, were formerly part of the military armour (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.6">1 Sam. xvii. 6</reference>): the use of them was to defend the feet against the gall-traps, and sharp sticks, which were wont to be laid privily in the way, to obstruct the marching of the enemy, those who fell upon them being unfit to march. <hi type="italic">The preparation of the gospel of peace</hi> signifies a prepared and resolved frame of heart, to adhere to the gospel and abide by it, which will enable us to walk with a steady pace in the way of religion, notwithstanding the difficulties and dangers that may be in it. It is styled <hi type="italic">the gospel of peace</hi> because it brings all sorts of peace, peace with God, with ourselves, and with one another. It may also be meant of that which prepares for the entertainment of the gospel, namely, repentance. With this our feet must be shod: for by living a life of repentance we are armed against temptations to sin, and the designs of our great enemy. Dr. Whitby thinks this may be the sense of the words: "That you may be ready for the combat, be shod with the gospel of peace, endeavour after that peaceable and quiet mind which the gospel calls for. Be not easily provoked, nor prone to quarrel: but show all gentleness and all long-suffering to all men, and this will certainly preserve you from many great temptations and persecutions, as did those shoes of brass the soldiers from those galltraps," &c. [4.] Faith must be our shield: <hi type="italic">Above all,</hi> or chiefly, <hi type="italic">taking the shield of faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.16">v. 16</reference>. This is more necessary than any of them. Faith is all in all to us in an hour of temptation. The breast-plate secures the vitals; but with the shield we turn every way. <hi type="italic">This is the victory over the world, even our faith.</hi> We are to be fully persuaded of the truth of all God's promises and threatenings, such a faith being of great use against temptations. Consider faith as it <hi type="italic">is the evidence of things not seen and the substance of things hoped for,</hi> and it will appear to be of admirable use for this purpose. Faith, as receiving Christ and the benefits of redemption, so deriving grace from him, is like a shield, a sort of universal defence. Our enemy the devil is here called <hi type="italic">the wicked one.</hi> He is wicked himself, and he endeavours to make us wicked. His temptations are called <hi type="italic">darts,</hi> because of their swift and undiscerned flight, and the deep wounds that they give to the soul; <hi type="italic">fiery darts,</hi> by way of allusion to the poisonous darts which were wont to inflame the parts which were wounded with them, and therefore were so called, as the serpents with poisonous stings are called fiery serpents. Violent temptations, by which the soul is set on fire of hell, are the darts which Satan shoots at us. Faith is the shield with which we must quench these fiery darts, wherein we should receive them, and so render them ineffectual, that they may not hit us, or at least that they may not hurt us. Observe, Faith, acted upon the word of God and applying that, acted upon the grace of Christ and improving that, quenches the darts of temptation. [5.] Salvation must be our helmet (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.17">v. 17</reference>); that is, <hi type="italic">hope,</hi> which has salvation for its object; so <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1 Thess. v. 8</reference>. The helmet secures the head. A good hope of salvation, well founded and well built, will both purify the soul and keep it from being defiled by Satan, and it will comfort the soul and keep it from being troubled and tormented by Satan. He would tempt us to despair; but good hope keeps us trusting in God, and rejoicing in him. [6.] The word of God is the sword of the Spirit. The sword is a very necessary and useful part of a soldier's furniture. The word of God is very necessary, and of great use to the Christian, in order to his maintaining the spiritual warfare and succeeding in it. It is called <hi type="italic">the sword of the Spirit,</hi> because it is of the Spirit's inditing and he renders it efficacious and powerful, and <hi type="italic">sharper than a two-edged sword.</hi> Like Goliath's sword, none like that; with this we assault the assailants. Scripture-arguments are the most powerful arguments to repel temptation with. Christ himself resisted Satan's temptations with, <hi type="italic">It is written,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.4.4">Matt. iv. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.7">7,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.10">10</reference>. This, being hid in the heart, will preserve from sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.11">Ps. cxix. 11</reference>), and will mortify and kill those lusts and corruptions that are latent there. [7.] Prayer must buckle on all the other parts of our Christian armour, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.18">v. 18</reference>. We must join prayer with all these graces, for our defence against these spiritual enemies, imploring help and assistance of God, as the case requires: and we must pray always. Not as though we were to do nothing else but pray, for there are other duties of religion and of our respective stations in the world that are to be done in their place and season; but we should keep up constant times of prayer, and be constant to them. We must pray upon all occasions, and as often as our own and others' necessities call us to it. We must always keep up a disposition to prayer, and should intermix ejaculatory prayers with other duties, and with common business. Though set and solemn prayer may sometimes be unseasonable (as when other duties are to be done), yet pious ejaculations <hi type="italic">can</hi> never be so. We must pray <hi type="italic">with all prayer and supplication,</hi> with all kinds of prayer: public, private, and secret, social and solitary, solemn and sudden; with all the parts of prayer: confession of sin, petition for mercy, and thanksgivings for favours received. We must pray <hi type="italic">in the Spirit;</hi> our spirits must be employed in the duty and we must do it by the grace of God's good Spirit. We must <hi type="italic">watch thereunto,</hi> endeavouring to keep our hearts in a praying frame, and taking all occasions, and improving all opportunities, for the duty: we must watch to all the motions of our own hearts towards the duty. When God says, <hi type="italic">Seek my face,</hi> our hearts must comply, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">Ps. xxvii. 8</reference>. This we must do <hi type="italic">with all perseverance.</hi> We must abide by the duty of prayer, whatever change there may be in our outward circumstances; and we must continue in it as long as we live in the world. We must persevere in a particular prayer; not cutting it short, when our hearts are disposed to enlarge, and there is time for it, and our occasions call for it. We must likewise persevere in particular requests, notwithstanding some present discouragements and repulses. And we must pray <hi type="italic">with supplication,</hi> not for ourselves only, but <hi type="italic">for all saints;</hi> for we are members one of another. Observe, None are so much saints, and in so good a condition in this world, but they need our prayers, and they ought to have them. The apostle passes hence to the conclusion of the epistle.
entries.f9f0703be152042da71d9ed8d1fdc49ee22b1f6f: <div eID="gen31901" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Conclusion. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31902" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, <hi type="super">20</hi> For which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak. <hi type="super">21</hi> But that ye also may know my affairs, <hi type="italic">and</hi> how I do, Tychicus, a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, shall make known to you all things: <hi type="super">22</hi> Whom I have sent unto you for the same purpose, that ye might know our affairs, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> he might comfort your hearts. <hi type="super">23</hi> Peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> with all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity. Amen. <div eID="gen31902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31903" type="x-p"/> Here, I. He desires their prayers for him, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">v. 19</reference>. Having mentioned <hi type="italic">supplication for all saints,</hi> he puts himself into the number. We must pray for all saints, and particularly for God's faithful ministers. <hi type="italic">Brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified.</hi> Observe what it is he would have them pray for in his behalf: "<hi type="italic">That utterance may be given unto me;</hi> that I may be enlarged from my present restraints, and so have liberty to propagate the faith of Christ; that I may have ability to express myself in a suitable and becoming manner; <hi type="italic">and that I may open my mouth boldly,</hi> that is, that I may deliver the whole counsel of God, without any base fear, shame, or partiality." <hi type="italic">To make known the mystery of the gospel;</hi> some understand it of that part of the gospel which concerns the calling of the Gentiles, which had hitherto, as a mystery, been concealed. But the whole gospel was a mystery, till made known by divine revelation; and it is the work of Christ's ministers to publish it. Observe, Paul had a great command of language; they called him Mercury, because he was the chief speaker (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.12">Acts xiv. 12</reference>), and yet he would have his friends ask of God the gift of utterance for him. He was a man of great courage, and often signalized himself for it; yet he would have them pray that God would give him boldness. He knew as well what to say as any man; yet he desires them to pray for him, that he may <hi type="italic">speak as he ought to speak.</hi> The argument with which he enforces his request is that for the sake of the gospel he was <hi type="italic">an ambassador in bonds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">v. 20</reference>. He was persecuted and imprisoned for preaching the gospel; though, notwithstanding, he continued in the embassy committed to him by Christ, and persisted in preaching it. Observe, 1. It is no new thing for Christ's ministers to be in bonds. 2. It is a hard thing for them to speak boldly when that is their case. 3. The best and most eminent ministers have need of, and may receive advantage by, the prayers of good Christians; and therefore should earnestly desire them. Having thus desired their prayers, <div eID="gen31903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31904" type="x-p"/> II. He recommends Tychicus unto them, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.21-Eph.6.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. He sent him with this epistle, that he might acquaint them with what other churches were informed of, namely, how he did, and what he did; how he was used by the Romans in his bonds, and how he behaved himself in his present circumstances. It is desirable to good ministers both that their Christian friends should know their state and that they should be acquainted with the condition of their friends; for by this means they may the better help each other in their prayers.—<hi type="italic">And that he might comfort their hearts,</hi> by giving such an account of his sufferings, of the cause of them, and of the temper of his mind and his behaviour under them, as might prevent their fainting at his tribulations and even minister matter of joy and thanksgiving unto them. He tells them that Tychicus was <hi type="italic">a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord.</hi> He was a sincere Christian, and so a brother in Christ: he was a faithful minister in the work of Christ, and he was very dear to Paul, which makes Paul's love to these Christian Ephesians the more observable, in that he should now part with so good and dear a friend for their sakes, when his company and conversation must have been peculiarly delightful and serviceable to himself. But the faithful servants of Jesus Christ are wont to prefer the public good to their own private or personal interests. <div eID="gen31904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31905" type="x-p"/> III. He concludes with his good wishes and prayers for them, and not for them only, but for all the brethren, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.23-Eph.6.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. His usual benediction was, <hi type="italic">Grace and peace;</hi> here it is, <hi type="italic">Peace be to the brethren, and love with faith.</hi> By peace we are to understand all manner of peace—peace with God, peace with conscience, peace among themselves: and all outward prosperity is included in the word; as if he had said, "I wish the continuance and increase of all happiness to you." <hi type="italic">And love with faith.</hi> This in part explains what he means in the <reference osisRef="Eph.6.24">following verse</reference> by grace; not only grace in the fountain, or the love and favour of God, but grace in the streams, the grace of the Spirit flowing from that divine principle, faith and love including all the rest. It is the continuance and increase of these that he desires for them, in whom they were already begun. It follows, <hi type="italic">from God the Father,</hi> &c. All Grace and blessings are derived to the saints from God, through the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ our Lord. The closing benediction is more extensive than the former; for in this he prays for all true believers at Ephesus, and every where else. It is the undoubted character of all the saints that they love our Lord Jesus Christ. Our love to Christ is not acceptable, unless it be in sincerity: indeed there is no such thing as love to Christ, whatever men may pretend, where there is not sincerity. The words may be read, <hi type="italic">Grace be with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption,</hi> who continue constant in their love to him, so as not to be corrupted out of it by any baits or seductions whatsoever, and whose love to him is uncorrupted by any opposite lust, or the love of any thing displeasing to him. Grace, that is, the favour of God, and all good (spiritual and temporal), that is, the product of it, are and shall be with all those who thus love our Lord Jesus Christ. And it is, or ought to be, the desire and prayer of every lover of Christ that it may be so with all his fellow-christians. <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> so be it.  <chapter eID="Eph.6"/> <div eID="gen31905" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen31796" osisID="Eph" type="book"/>

entries.1d1e4b26a55f174c07321d913a7ba5a37398cddf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17700"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Eph.6.1-Eph.6.24">Ep 6:1-24</reference>. Mutual Duties of Parents and Children: Masters and Servants: Our Life a Warfare: The Spiritual Armour Needed against Spiritual Foes. Conclusion.</title> <div sID="gen35783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17700"/><hi type="bold">1. obey--</hi>stronger than the expression as to wives, "submitting," or "being subject" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.21">Ep 5:21</reference>). Obedience is more unreasoning and implicit; submission is the willing subjection of an inferior in point of order to one who has a right to command.<div eID="gen35783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord--</hi>Both parents and children being Christians "in the Lord," expresses the element in which the obedience is to take place, and the motive to obedience. In <reference osisRef="Col.3.20">Col 3:20</reference>, it is, "Children, obey your parents in all things." This clause, "in the Lord," would suggest the due limitation of the obedience required (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.29">Ac 5:29</reference>; compare on the other hand, the abuse, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.11-Mark.7.13">Mr 7:11-13</reference>).<div eID="gen35784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right--</hi>Even by natural law we should render obedience to them from whom we have derived life. <div eID="gen35785" type="x-p"/>
entries.58146c5acd57ca676402578b334fae4c335da697: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17701"/><div sID="gen35786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17701"/>2. Here the authority of revealed law is added to that of natural law.<div eID="gen35786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is ... promise--</hi>The "promise" is not made the main motive to obedience, but an incidental one. The main motive is, because it is God's will (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.16">De 5:16</reference>, "Honor thy father and mother, as the Lord thy God hath COMMANDED thee"); and that it is so peculiarly, is shown by His accompanying it "with a promise."<div eID="gen35787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first--</hi>in the decalogue with a special promise. The promise in the second commandment is a general one. Their duty is more expressly prescribed to children than to parents; for love descends rather than ascends [Bengel]. This verse proves the law in the Old Testament is not abolished. <div eID="gen35788" type="x-p"/>
entries.d56e995917e4df106b5f232a9984f0126e9d89bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17702"/><div sID="gen35789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17702"/><hi type="bold">3. long on the earth--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Exod.20.12">Ex 20:12</reference>, "long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee," which Paul adapts to Gospel times, by taking away the local and limited reference peculiar to the Jews in Canaan. The godly are equally blessed in every land, as the Jews were in the land which God gave them. This promise is always fulfilled, either literally, or by the substitution of a higher blessing, namely, one spiritual and eternal (<reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.27">Pr 10:27</reference>). The substance and essence of the law are eternally in force: its accidents alone (applying to Israel of old) are abolished (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.15">Ro 6:15</reference>). <div eID="gen35789" type="x-p"/>
entries.4dad09000f6a7f549b89757f6a04d3f9abe30c08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17703"/><div sID="gen35790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17703"/><hi type="bold">4. fathers--</hi>including mothers; the fathers are specified as being the fountains of domestic authority. Fathers are more prone to passion in relation to their children than mothers, whose fault is rather over-indulgence.<div eID="gen35790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">provoke not--</hi>irritate not, by vexatious commands, unreasonable blame, and uncertain temper [Alford]. <reference osisRef="Col.3.21">Col 3:21</reference>, "lest they be discouraged."<div eID="gen35791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nurture--</hi>Greek, "discipline," namely, training by chastening in act where needed (<reference osisRef="Job.5.17">Job 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.7">He 12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen35792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">admonition--</hi>training by words (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">De 6:7</reference>; "catechise," <reference osisRef="Prov.22.6">Pr 22:6</reference>, Margin), whether of encouragement, or remonstrance, or reproof, according as is required [Trench]. Contrast <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.13">1Sa 3:13</reference>, Margin.<div eID="gen35793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the Lord--</hi>such as the Lord approves, and by His Spirit dictates. <div eID="gen35794" type="x-p"/>
entries.1dff454e082c008dff06f8031d1f5f14a9d94df5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17704"/><div sID="gen35795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17704"/><hi type="bold">5. Servants--</hi>literally, "slaves."<div eID="gen35795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">masters according to the flesh--</hi>in contrast to your true and heavenly Master (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.4">Ep 6:4</reference>). A consolatory him that the mastership to which they were subject, was but for a time [Chrysostom]; and that their real liberty was still their own (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>).<div eID="gen35796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fear and trembling--</hi>not slavish terror, but (See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.3">1Co 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.15">2Co 7:15</reference>) an anxious eagerness to do your duty, and a fear of displeasing, as great as is produced in the ordinary slave by "threatenings" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">Ep 6:9</reference>).<div eID="gen35797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">singleness--</hi>without double-mindedness, or "eye service" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.6">Ep 6:6</reference>), which seeks to please outwardly, without the sincere desire to make the master's interest at all times the first consideration (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.17">1Ch 29:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.22">Mt 6:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.34">Lu 11:34</reference>). "Simplicity." <div eID="gen35798" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b2b2892829cc04a5aac72b0bff113744ae44af4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17705"/><div sID="gen35799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17705"/>6. (<reference osisRef="Col.3.22">Col 3:22</reference>). Seeking to please their masters only so long as these have their eyes on them: as Gehazi was a very different man in his master's presence from what he was in his absence (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.1-2Kgs.5.18">2Ki 5:1-18</reference>).<div eID="gen35799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men-pleasers--</hi>not Christ-pleasers (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Ga 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.4">1Th 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen35800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doing the will of God--</hi>the unseen but ever present Master: the best guarantee for your serving faithfully your earthly master alike when present and when absent.<div eID="gen35801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the heart--</hi>literally, soul (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.1">Psa 111:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.5">Ro 13:5</reference>). <div eID="gen35802" type="x-p"/>
entries.04970aa1acb056fe70a1c5d62efebf5699f895f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17706"/><div sID="gen35803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17706"/><hi type="bold">7. good will--</hi>expressing his feeling towards his master; as "doing the will of God from the heart" expresses the source of that feeling (<reference osisRef="Col.3.23">Col 3:23</reference>). "Good will" is stated by Xenophon [Economics] to be the principal virtue of a slave towards his master: a real regard to his master's interest as if his own, a good will which not even a master's severity can extinguish. <div eID="gen35803" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9e087be3f7756eb73b43fc582f049035fe3cb84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17707"/><div sID="gen35804" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17707"/><hi type="bold">8. any man doeth--</hi>Greek, "any man shall have done," that is, shall be found at the Lord's coming to have done.<div eID="gen35804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same--</hi>in full payment, in heaven's currency.<div eID="gen35805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall ... receive--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">2Co 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.25">Col 3:25</reference>; but all of grace, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.10">Lu 17:10</reference>).<div eID="gen35806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bond or free--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.13">12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col 3:11</reference>). Christ does not regard such distinctions in His present dealings of grace, or in His future judgment. The slave that has acted faithfully for the Lord's sake to his master, though the latter may not repay his faithfulness, shall have the Lord for his Paymaster. So the freeman who has done good for the Lord's sake, though man may not pay him, has the Lord for his Debtor (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.17">Pr 19:17</reference>). <div eID="gen35807" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb104ae1be87a761991839a50a6183477dce739d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17708"/><div sID="gen35808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17708"/><hi type="bold">9. the same things--</hi>Mutatis mutandis. Show the same regard to God's will, and to your servants' well-being, in your relation to them, as they ought to have in their relation to you. Love regulates the duties both of servants and masters, as one and the same light attempers various colors. Equality of nature and faith is superior to distinctions of rank [Bengel]. Christianity makes all men brothers: compare <reference osisRef="Lev.25.42">Le 25:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.43">43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12">De 15:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.14">Jr 34:14</reference> as to how the Hebrews were bound to treat their brethren in service; much more ought Christians to act with love.<div eID="gen35808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threatening--</hi>Greek, "the threatening" which masters commonly use. "Masters" in the Greek, is not so strong a term as "despots": it implies authority, but not absolute domination.<div eID="gen35809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your Master also--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "the Master both of them and you": "their Master and yours." This more forcibly brings out the equality of slaves and masters in the sight of God. Seneca [Thyestes, 607], says, "Whatever an inferior dreads from you, this a superior Master threatens yourselves with: every authority here is under a higher above." As you treat your servants, so will He treat you.<div eID="gen35810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... respect of persons--</hi>He will not, in judging, acquit thee because thou art a master, or condemn him because he is a servant (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.34">Ac 10:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.11">Ro 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.6">Ga 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.25">Col 3:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.17">1Pe 1:17</reference>). Derived from <reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">De 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.7">2Ch 19:7</reference>. <div eID="gen35811" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea488200b90a6299f2b6b9e489fbd8541f4487fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17709"/><div sID="gen35812" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17709"/><hi type="bold">10. my brethren--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts omit these words. Some with Vulgate retain them. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Epistle (see, however, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.23">Ep 6:23</reference>); if genuine, it is appropriate here in the close of the Epistle, where he is urging his fellow soldiers to the good fight in the Christian armor. Most of the oldest manuscripts for "finally," read, "henceforward," or "from henceforth" (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.17">Ga 6:17</reference>).<div eID="gen35812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be strong--</hi>Greek, "be strengthened."<div eID="gen35813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the power of his might--</hi>Christ's might: as in <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, it is the Father's might. <div eID="gen35814" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5e49a5e0f6806ce5a9bd27af43dabea51fea3fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17710"/><div sID="gen35815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17710"/><hi type="bold">11. the whole armour--</hi>the armor of light (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Ro 13:12</reference>); on the right hand and left (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.7">2Co 6:7</reference>). The panoply offensive and defensive. An image readily suggested by the Roman armory, Paul being now in Rome. Repeated emphatically, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">Ep 6:13</reference>. In <reference osisRef="Rom.13.14">Ro 13:14</reference> it is, "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ"; in putting on Him, and the new man in Him, we put on "the whole armor of God." No opening at the head, the feet, the heart, the belly, the eye, the ear, or the tongue, is to be given to Satan. Believers have once for all overcome him; but on the ground of this fundamental victory gained over him, they are ever again to fight against and overcome him, even as they who once die with Christ have continually to mortify their members upon earth (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.2-Rom.6.14">Ro 6:2-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen35815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>furnished by God; not our own, else it would not stand (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.1-Ps.35.3">Psa 35:1-3</reference>). Spiritual, therefore, and mighty through God, not carnal (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>).<div eID="gen35816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wiles--</hi>literally, "schemes sought out" for deceiving (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.14">2Co 11:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the devil--</hi>the ruling chief of the foes (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>) organized into a kingdom of darkness (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.26">Mt 12:26</reference>), opposed to the kingdom of light. <div eID="gen35818" type="x-p"/>
entries.f17472f4c6581a13bb9e9ca9c54d0496971adf25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17711"/><div sID="gen35819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17711"/>12. Greek, "For our wrestling ('the wrestling' in which we are engaged) is not against flesh," &c. Flesh and blood foes are Satan's mere tools, the real foe lurking behind them is Satan himself, with whom our conflict is. "Wrestling" implies that it is a hand-to-hand and foot-to-foot struggle for the mastery: to wrestle successfully with Satan, we must wrestle with God in irresistible prayer like Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.24-Gen.32.29">Ge 32:24-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.4">Ho 12:4</reference>). Translate, "The principalities ... the powers" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Ep 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>). The same grades of powers are specified in the case of the demons here, as in that of angels there (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1Co 15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col 2:15</reference>). The Ephesians had practiced sorcery (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.19">Ac 19:19</reference>), so that he appropriately treats of evil spirits in addressing them. The more clearly any book of Scripture, as this, treats of the economy of the kingdom of light, the more clearly does it set forth the kingdom of darkness. Hence, nowhere does the satanic kingdom come more clearly into view than in the Gospels which treat of Christ, the true Light.<div eID="gen35819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rulers of the darkness of this world--</hi>Greek, "age" or "course of the world." But the oldest manuscripts omit "of world." Translate, "Against the world rulers of this (present) darkness" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.8">5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.53">Lu 22:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col 1:13</reference>). On Satan and his demons being "world rulers," compare <reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.30">14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.11">16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.6">Lu 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1Jo 5:19</reference>, Greek, "lieth in the wicked one." Though they be "world rulers," they are not the ruler of the universe; and their usurped rule of the world is soon to cease, when He shall "come whose right it is" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>). Two cases prove Satan not to be a mere subjective fancy: (1) Christ's temptation; (2) the entrance of demons into the swine (for these are incapable of such fancies). Satan tries to parody, or imitate in a perverted way, God's working (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.14">14</reference>). So when God became incarnate, Satan, by his demons, took forcible possession of human bodies. Thus the demoniacally possessed were not peculiarly wicked, but miserable, and so fit subjects for Jesus' pity. Paul makes no mention of demoniacal possession, so that in the time he wrote, it seems to have ceased; it probably was restricted to the period of the Lord's incarnation, and of the foundation of His Church.<div eID="gen35820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spiritual wickedness--</hi>rather as Greek, "The spiritual hosts of wickedness." As three of the clauses describe the power, so this fourth, the wickedness of our spiritual foes (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.45">Mt 12:45</reference>).<div eID="gen35821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in high places--</hi>Greek, "heavenly places": in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>, "the air," see on <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>. The alteration of expression to "in heavenly places," is in order to mark the higher range of their powers than ours, they having been, up to the ascension (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.5">Re 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.10">9, 10</reference>), dwellers "in the heavenly places" (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job 1:7</reference>), and being now in the regions of the air which are called the heavens. Moreover, pride and presumption are the sins in heavenly places to which they tempt especially, being those by which they themselves fell from heavenly places (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.12-Isa.14.15">Is 14:12-15</reference>). But believers have naught to fear, being "blessed with all spiritual blessings in the heavenly places" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen35822" type="x-p"/>
entries.02fea28d123ba02d8fcd3c48878cd78670604fdb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17712"/><div sID="gen35823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17712"/><hi type="bold">13. take ... of God--</hi>not "make," God has done that: you have only to "take up" and put it on. The Ephesians were familiar with the idea of the gods giving armor to mythical heroes: thus Paul's allusion would be appropriate.<div eID="gen35823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the evil day--</hi>the day of Satan's special assaults (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.16">16</reference>) in life and at the dying hour (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.3.10">Re 3:10</reference>). We must have our armor always on, to be ready against the evil day which may come at any moment, the war being perpetual (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Psa 41:1</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen35824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">done all--</hi>rather, "accomplished all things," namely, necessary to the fight, and becoming a good soldier. <div eID="gen35825" type="x-p"/>
entries.55144c5e786fd92c75555063c5334e85d1e4b33a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17713"/><div sID="gen35826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17713"/><hi type="bold">14. Stand--</hi>The repetition in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">Ep 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.14">14</reference>, shows that standing, that is, maintaining our ground, not yielding or fleeing, is the grand aim of the Christian soldier. Translate as Greek, "Having girt about your loins with truth," that is, with truthfulness, sincerity, a good conscience (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2Co 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">3:9</reference>). Truth is the band that girds up and keeps together the flowing robes, so as that the Christian soldier may be unencumbered for action. So the Passover was eaten with the loins girt, and the shoes on the feet (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.11">Ex 12:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.27">Is 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.35">Lu 12:35</reference>). Faithfulness (Septuagint, "truth") is the girdle of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.5">Is 11:5</reference>): so truth of His followers.<div eID="gen35826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having on--</hi>Greek, "having put on."<div eID="gen35827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breastplate of righteousness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Is 59:17</reference>), similarly of Messiah. "Righteousness" is here joined with "truth," as in <reference osisRef="Eph.5.9">Ep 5:9</reference>: righteousness in works, truth in words [Estius] (<reference osisRef="1John.3.7">1Jo 3:7</reference>). Christ's righteousness inwrought in us by the Spirit. "Faith and love," that is, faith working righteousness by love, are "the breastplate" in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:8</reference>. <div eID="gen35828" type="x-p"/>
entries.7314dbc837c566e80f886a373ca3c07d50a4e2a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17714"/><div sID="gen35829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17714"/>15. Translate, "Having shod your feet" (referring to the sandals, or to the military shoes then used).<div eID="gen35829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the preparation--</hi>rather, "the preparedness," or "readiness of," that is, arising from the "Gospel" (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Psa 10:17</reference>). Preparedness to do and suffer all that God wills; readiness for march, as a Christian soldier.<div eID="gen35830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gospel of peace--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.79">Lu 1:79</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Ro 10:15</reference>). The "peace" within forms a beautiful contrast to the raging of the outward conflict (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Is 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Php 4:7</reference>). <div eID="gen35831" type="x-p"/>
entries.c514ee4ca292d669ff2dd5bd110a8b7fd91c377a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17715"/><div sID="gen35832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17715"/><hi type="bold">16. Above all--</hi>rather, "Over all"; so as to cover all that has been put on before. Three integuments are specified, the breastplate, girdle, and shoes; two defenses, the helmet and shield; and two offensive weapons, the sword and the spear (prayer). Alford translates, "Besides all," as the Greek is translated, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.20">Lu 3:20</reference>. But if it meant this, it would have come last in the list (compare <reference osisRef="Col.3.14">Col 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shield--</hi>the large oblong oval door-like shield of the Romans, four feet long by two and a half feet broad; not the small round buckler.<div eID="gen35833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall be able--</hi>not merely, "ye may." The shield of faith will certainly intercept, and so "quench, all the fiery darts" (an image from the ancient fire-darts, formed of cane, with tow and combustibles ignited on the head of the shaft, so as to set fire to woodwork, tents, &c.).<div eID="gen35834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the wicked--</hi>rather "of the EVIL ONE." Faith conquers him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">1Pe 5:9</reference>), and his darts of temptation to wrath, lust, revenge, despair, &c. It overcomes the world (<reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1Jo 5:4</reference>), and so the prince of the world (<reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1Jo 5:18</reference>). <div eID="gen35835" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3d6207f07d82f7db4d50c4b64884187af57b889: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17716"/><div sID="gen35836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17716"/><hi type="bold">17. take--</hi>a different Greek word from that in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">Ep 6:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.16">16</reference>; translate, therefore, "receive," "accept," namely, the helmet offered by the Lord, namely, "salvation" appropriated, as <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:8</reference>, "Helmet, the hope of salvation"; not an uncertain hope, but one that brings with it no shame of disappointment (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>). It is subjoined to the shield of faith, as being its inseparable accompaniment (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">5</reference>). The head of the soldier was among the principal parts to be defended, as on it the deadliest strokes might fall, and it is the head that commands the whole body. The head is the seat of the mind, which, when it has laid hold of the sure Gospel "hope" of eternal life, will not receive false doctrine, or give way to Satan's temptations to despair. God, by this hope, "lifts up the head" (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">Lu 21:28</reference>).<div eID="gen35836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword of the Spirit--</hi>that is, furnished by the Spirit, who inspired the writers of the word of God (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2Pe 1:21</reference>). Again the Trinity is implied: the Spirit here; and Christ in "salvation" and God the Father, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">Ep 6:13</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.16">Re 1:16</reference>; 2:12). The two-edged sword, cutting both ways (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.3">Psa 45:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">5</reference>), striking some with conviction and conversion, and others with condemnation (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">Re 19:15</reference>), is in the mouth of Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Is 49:2</reference>), in the hand of His saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.6">Psa 149:6</reference>). Christ's use of this sword in the temptation is our pattern as to how we are to wield it against Satan (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.4">Mt 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.10">7, 10</reference>). There is no armor specified for the back, but only for the front of the body; implying that we must never turn our back to the foe (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.62">Lu 9:62</reference>); our only safety is in resisting ceaselessly (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.11">Mt 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.7">Jas 4:7</reference>). <div eID="gen35837" type="x-p"/>
entries.e617f00e9269fcc0347528a77c989334542b0923: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17717"/><div sID="gen35838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17717"/><hi type="bold">18. always--</hi>Greek, "in every season"; implying opportunity and exigency (<reference osisRef="Col.4.2">Col 4:2</reference>). Paul uses the very words of Jesus in <reference osisRef="Luke.21.36">Lu 21:36</reference> (a Gospel which he quotes elsewhere, in undesigned consonance with the fact of Luke being his associate in travel, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">1Ti 5:18</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.18.1">Lu 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.12">Ro 12:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.17">1Th 5:17</reference>.<div eID="gen35838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with all--</hi>that is, every kind of.<div eID="gen35839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prayer--</hi>a sacred term for prayer in general.<div eID="gen35840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">supplication--</hi>a common term for a special kind of prayer [Harless], an imploring request. "Prayer" for obtaining blessings, "supplication" for averting evils which we fear [Grotius].<div eID="gen35841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Spirit--</hi>to be joined with "praying." It is he in us, as the Spirit of adoption, who prays, and enables us to pray (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Ro 8:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Ga 4:6</reference>; Jude 20).<div eID="gen35842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watching--</hi>not sleeping (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.13">Psa 88:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.41">Mt 26:41</reference>). So in the temple a perpetual watch was maintained (compare Anna, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.37">Lu 2:37</reference>).<div eID="gen35843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thereunto--</hi>"watching unto" (with a view to) prayer and supplication.<div eID="gen35844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>Greek, "in." Persevering constancy ("perseverance") and (that is, exhibited in) supplication are to be the element in which our watchfulness is to be exercised.<div eID="gen35845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for all saints--</hi>as none is so perfect as not to need the intercessions of his fellow Christians. <div eID="gen35846" type="x-p"/>
entries.cafa345e1f34fc8b9e9e2bc5af60e20fce3a25bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17718"/><div sID="gen35847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17718"/><hi type="bold">19. for me--</hi>a different Greek preposition from that in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.18">Ep 6:18</reference>; translate, therefore, "on my behalf."<div eID="gen35847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I may open my mouth boldly--</hi>rather, "that there may be given to me 'utterance,' or 'speech' in the opening of my mouth (when I undertake to speak; a formula used in set and solemn speech, <reference osisRef="Job.3.1">Job 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.16">Da 10:16</reference>), so as with boldness to make known," &c. Bold plainness of speech was the more needed, as the Gospel is a "mystery" undiscoverable by mere reason, and only known by revelation. Paul looked for utterance to be given him; he did not depend on his natural or acquired power. The shortest road to any heart is by way of heaven; pray to God to open the door and to open your mouth, so as to avail yourself of every opening (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.7">Jr 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.8">Eze 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.11">9, 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13">2Co 4:13</reference>). <div eID="gen35848" type="x-p"/>
entries.371ef19345838b7dc4d9889a39aa9e42ee21475f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17719"/><div sID="gen35849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17719"/><hi type="bold">20. For--</hi>Greek, as in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, "On behalf of which."<div eID="gen35849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an ambassador in bonds--</hi>a paradox. Ambassadors were held inviolable by the law of nations, and could not, without outrage to every sacred right, be put in chains. Yet Christ's "ambassador is in a chain!" The Greek is singular. The Romans used to bind a prisoner to a soldier by a single chain, in a kind of free custody. So <reference osisRef="Acts.28.16">Ac 28:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.28.20">20</reference>, "I am bound with this chain." The term, "bonds" (plural), on the other hand, is used when the prisoner's hands or feet were bound together (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.29">Ac 26:29</reference>); compare <reference osisRef="Acts.12.6">Ac 12:6</reference>, where the plural marks the distinction. The singular is only used of the particular kind of custody described above; an undesigned coincidence [Paley]. <div eID="gen35850" type="x-p"/>
entries.1db156c774b56de6b21734c80cd17369732a5d3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17720"/><div sID="gen35851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17720"/><hi type="bold">21. that ye also--</hi>as I have been discussing things relating to you, so that ye also may know about me (compare <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">8</reference>). Neander takes it, "Ye also," as well as the Colossians (<reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen35851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my affairs--</hi>Greek, "the things concerning me."<div eID="gen35852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how I do--</hi>how I fare.<div eID="gen35853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tychicus--</hi>an Asiatic, and so a fit messenger bearing the respective Epistles to Ephesus and Colosse (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">Ac 20:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen35854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a beloved brother--</hi>Greek, "the beloved brother"; the same epithet as in <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>.<div eID="gen35855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">minister--</hi>that is, servant.<div eID="gen35856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord--</hi>in the Lord's work. <div eID="gen35857" type="x-p"/>
entries.41a0ba826c9bcb15a4cfd5d65dd4d56d2b94ecc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17721"/><div sID="gen35858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17721"/><hi type="bold">22. for the same purpose--</hi>Greek, "for this very purpose." <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">Col 4:8</reference> is almost word for word the same as this verse.<div eID="gen35858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35859" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our affairs--</hi>Greek, "the things concerning us," namely, concerning myself. "Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen35859" type="x-p"/>
